92035.e: Only with direct current does each pole always stay plus or always minus. So the same gas always forms at each electrode and can be collected separately.

92036.q: In what volume ratio do hydrogen and oxygen form in the electrolysis of water?
92036.e: Every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So twice as much hydrogen gas forms as oxygen gas.
92036.m: Electrolysis of water produces twice as much hydrogen as oxygen.

92037.q: Which energy conversion takes place in electrolysis?
92037.e: In electrolysis, an electric current forces a chemical reaction. The energy is then stored in the products of the reaction.
92037.m: Electrolysis stores electrical energy in substances.

92038.q: What is the positive pole in electrolysis called?
92038.e: The positive pole is called the anode, the negative one the cathode. At the anode, particles give up electrons.
92038.m: In electrolysis, the anode is the positive pole.

92039.q: How can you tell that a reaction is taking place in the electrolysis of water?
92039.e: Bubbles rise at both poles. Hydrogen forms at one pole and oxygen at the other.
92039.m: In the electrolysis of water, gas bubbles form at the poles.

92040.q: Why do you add a little acid or salt to the water for electrolysis?
a: Because pure water conducts electricity poorly
So that the water does not freeze
So that the gases become coloured
92040.e: Pure water contains only very few ions. Acid or salt provide extra ions that conduct the current.
92040.m: Ions in the water are what make electrolysis really work.

92041.q: Which device reverses the electrolysis of water and produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen?
92041.e: In a fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen react in a controlled way to form water. Electrical energy is released.
92041.m: A fuel cell produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.

92042.q: Which metal was produced using electrolysis at Neuhausen am Rheinfall from 1888?
92042.e: Aluminium can only be obtained with a lot of electricity by molten salt electrolysis. The water power of the Rhine Falls supplied the energy needed.
92042.m: Aluminium is obtained by electrolysis using a lot of electricity.

92043.q: What is hydrogen made by electrolysis using electricity from renewable energy called?
92043.e: If the electricity for electrolysis comes from sun, wind or water power, hardly any CO2 is produced. Hydrogen from natural gas, by contrast, is called grey.
92043.m: Green hydrogen is made with renewable electricity.

92044.q: Which dissolved particles make water hard?
92044.e: On its way through the ground, water dissolves calcium and magnesium out of the rock. The more of these is dissolved, the harder the water.
92044.m: Calcium and magnesium decide how hard water is.

92045.q: What is water called from which practically all dissolved salts have been removed, for example for a steam iron?
92045.e: In distilling, water is evaporated and the steam condensed again. The dissolved salts stay behind, so this water forms no limescale.
92045.m: Distilled water contains almost no dissolved salts.

92046.q: Which substance builds up in the kettle with hard water?
92046.e: When hard water is heated, calcium carbonate comes out of it. This white layer is called limescale or scale.
92046.m: Hard water leaves limescale in the kettle.

92047.q: How does an ion exchanger soften water?
a: It filters out sand and gravel
92047.e: In the ion exchanger, calcium and magnesium ions are held on a resin. In return, the resin releases sodium ions, which do not form limescale.
92047.m: An ion exchanger makes hard water soft.

92048.q: What is the chemical formula of limestone (calcium carbonate)?
92048.e: Calcium carbonate consists of calcium, carbon and oxygen. In nature it occurs as limestone, marble and chalk.
92048.m: Calcium carbonate has the formula CaCO3.

92049.q: What is spring water usually like if it has only flowed through granite and gneiss?
92049.e: Granite and gneiss contain hardly any lime that could dissolve. So water from such areas, for example in parts of the Alps, tends to be soft.
92049.m: Water from rock with little lime is soft.

92050.q: Why does soap lather poorly in very hard water?
a: It forms insoluble scum with calcium
92050.e: The calcium ions combine with the soap to form an insoluble coating. Some of the soap then no longer works.
92050.m: In hard water you need more soap.

92051.q: What does it mean if the tap water where you live is very hard?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
It contains a lot of sugar
It is as sour as vinegar
92051.e: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved calcium and magnesium. So it quickly forms limescale in the kettle.
92051.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

92052.q: Roughly what is the density of ice?
92052.e: Ice weighs about 0.92 grams per cubic centimetre, which makes it lighter than liquid water. So a litre of ice weighs only about 920 grams.
92052.m: Ice is a little lighter than liquid water.

92053.q: Why does ice float on water?
a: Ice has a lower density than water
Ice contains air bubbles of nitrogen
Ice is lighter because it is cold
Ice is carried by the wind
92053.e: When water freezes, its molecules arrange themselves in a loose lattice. So ice takes up more space and is lighter than the same amount of liquid water.
92053.m: Ice floats because it is less dense than water.

92054.q: Why can fish survive the winter in a frozen lake?
a: The lake freezes from the top down
The water only freezes at night
92054.e: The coldest water stays at the top and freezes first. The layer of ice insulates, and liquid water remains at the bottom.
92054.m: Lakes freeze from the top, so fish survive the winter.

92055.q: By roughly how much does the volume of water increase when it freezes?
92055.e: 100 litres of water become about 109 litres of ice. This expansion is very unusual for a liquid.
92055.m: Freezing water expands by about a tenth.

92056.q: What is the process called in which freezing water breaks up rocks in the Alps?
92056.e: Water gets into cracks in the rock. When it freezes, it expands and pushes the cracks apart until pieces break off.
92056.m: In frost shattering, freezing water breaks up rock.

92057.q: Why can a full, closed glass bottle of water burst in the freezer?
a: Overpressure builds up in the freezer
92057.e: Ice needs more space than liquid water. In a full bottle it has no room and bursts the glass.
92057.m: Full water bottles burst when they freeze.

92059.q: Roughly what part of an iceberg lies below the surface of the water?
92059.e: Ice is only a little lighter than sea water. So only about a tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the water.
92059.m: You only see the tip of an iceberg.

92060.q: Where does about 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water come from?
92060.e: About 40 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and about 40 per cent from groundwater. The remaining 20 per cent or so is taken from lakes.
92060.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from underground.

92061.q: How can germs in drinking water be killed without adding any chemicals?
92061.e: Ultraviolet light damages the genetic material of bacteria and viruses so that they can no longer multiply. Many Swiss water suppliers use this method.
92061.m: UV light disinfects water without chemicals.

92062.q: What job does a sand filter do in a waterworks?
92062.e: The water trickles slowly through layers of sand and gravel. Cloudy matter and fine particles get caught.
92062.m: Sand filters make cloudy water clear.

92063.q: What is activated carbon used for in treating drinking water?
a: To bind smells and trace substances
92063.e: Activated carbon has a huge inner surface with many pores. Substances that spoil the taste and smell, as well as many residues, stick to it.
92063.m: Activated carbon binds unwanted substances on its large surface.

92064.q: Which substance is sometimes added to the water mains so that the water stays free of germs all the way to the tap?
92064.e: A small amount of chlorine or chlorine dioxide keeps working against germs in the pipes. But in many Swiss municipalities the water is so clean that this is not needed.
92064.m: Chlorine can keep drinking water germ-free in the pipes.

92065.q: Which gas with three oxygen atoms is used for disinfection in lake waterworks?
92065.e: Ozone (O3) is a very strong oxidising agent. It kills germs and breaks down many smelly substances and pollutants.
92065.m: Ozone is used to disinfect lake water.

92066.q: What does a flocculant do in water treatment?
92066.e: The flocculant makes tiny floating particles clump into larger flakes. These can then easily settle or be filtered out.
92066.m: Flocculants make small dirt particles filterable.

92067.q: From which body of water does the city of Zurich get most of its drinking water?
92067.e: About 70 per cent of Zurich’s drinking water comes from Lake Zurich. It is treated in several stages at the Lengg and Moos lake waterworks.
92067.m: Zurich mainly drinks treated lake water.

92068.q: What is the most important solvent on Earth?
92068.e: Water dissolves very many substances, such as salts, sugar and gases. In our bodies and in nature, almost all chemical processes take place in water.
92068.m: Water is the most important solvent.

92069.q: Which of these substances dissolves well in water?
92069.e: Salts are made of ions that get surrounded by water molecules. Fats and waxes, on the other hand, do not dissolve in water.
92069.m: Table salt dissolves well in water, but fat does not.

92070.q: Which solvent is found in many nail varnish removers?
92070.e: Acetone quickly dissolves the plastics in nail varnish. It evaporates fast and catches fire easily.
92070.m: Acetone is a well-known solvent for nail varnish.

92071.q: What do you call a solution in which no more of a substance will dissolve at the same temperature?
92071.e: In a saturated solution, the largest possible amount of a substance is dissolved. If you add more, it stays at the bottom as sediment.
92071.m: Nothing more dissolves in a saturated solution.

92072.q: Why does warm fizzy mineral water lose its fizz faster than cold?
a: Gases dissolve less well when warm
The bottle seals better when warm
92072.e: Unlike sugar or salt, gases become less soluble as the temperature rises. So the dissolved carbon dioxide escapes faster.
92072.m: Gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm.

92073.q: Why is water so good at dissolving salts?
92073.e: A water molecule has a slightly negative end and a slightly positive end. This lets it surround positive and negative ions and pull them out of the salt crystal.
92073.m: Polar water molecules pull ions out of salt crystals.

92074.q: How does sugar dissolve faster in tea?
a: By stirring it in hot tea
By leaving it still in cold tea
With an ice cube in the tea
With a lid on the cup
92074.e: Heat and stirring get the particles moving. That way the sugar dissolves much faster.
92074.m: Heat and stirring speed up dissolving.

92075.q: What removes a grease stain better than plain water?
a: A non-polar solvent such as white spirit
92075.e: Following the rule “like dissolves like”, non-polar fats dissolve in non-polar solvents. Water, by contrast, is polar.
92075.m: Fat dissolves in non-polar solvents, not in water.

92076.q: You dissolve 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the salt?
92076.e: The solution weighs 20 g + 180 g = 200 g. The mass fraction is 20 g ÷ 200 g = 0.10, so 10 %.
92076.m: For the mass fraction, you divide by the mass of the whole solution.

92077.q: How much sugar do 500 g of a sugar solution with a mass fraction of 5 % contain?
92077.e: You work out 5 % of 500 g as 500 g times 0.05. That gives 25 g of sugar.
92077.m: The mass of the dissolved substance is the mass fraction times the mass of the solution.

92078.q: You dissolve 50 g of sugar in 200 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the sugar?
92078.e: The solution weighs 50 g + 200 g = 250 g. The mass fraction is 50 g ÷ 250 g = 0.20, so 20 %.
92078.m: The solvent also counts towards the total mass of the solution.

92079.q: How do you calculate the mass fraction of a substance in a mixture?
a: Mass of the substance divided by mass of the mixture
Mass of the mixture divided by mass of the substance
Mass of the substance times volume of the mixture
Volume of the substance divided by its mass
92079.e: The mass fraction tells you what share of the total mass belongs to one substance. You divide the mass of the substance by the mass of the whole mixture.
92079.m: The mass fraction is a ratio of two masses.

92080.q: Sea water has a salt mass fraction of about 3.5 %. How much salt do 2 kg of sea water contain?
92080.e: 2 kg is 2000 g. 2000 g times 0.035 gives 70 g of salt.
92080.m: Sea water contains about 35 grams of salt per kilogram.

92081.q: You add 200 g of water to 300 g of a 10 per cent salt solution. What is the new mass fraction?
92081.e: The solution contains 300 g times 0.10 = 30 g of salt. After diluting it weighs 500 g, so the share is 30 g ÷ 500 g = 6 %.
92081.m: When diluting, the mass of the dissolved substance stays the same.

92082.q: You dissolve 12 g of salt in 228 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the salt?
92082.e: The solution weighs 12 g + 228 g = 240 g. The mass fraction is 12 g ÷ 240 g = 0.05, so 5 %.
92082.m: First work out the mass of the whole solution.

92083.q: How much water do you need to make 400 g of a salt solution with a mass fraction of 15 %?
92083.e: The solution contains 400 g times 0.15 = 60 g of salt. The rest is water: 400 g minus 60 g = 340 g.
92083.m: The mass of the solvent is the total mass minus the mass of the dissolved substance.

92084.q: Roughly what is the mass fraction of oxygen in water (H2O), if H has a mass of 1 u and O a mass of 16 u?
92084.e: A water molecule has a mass of 2 times 1 u + 16 u = 18 u. The oxygen share is 16 ÷ 18, about 0.89, so around 89 %.
92084.m: By mass, water is mostly oxygen.

92184.e: Blaise Pascal started building this machine in 1642. It could add numbers and was named after him.
92184.m: The Pascaline was invented by Blaise Pascal.

92185.q: Who did Blaise Pascal originally build his calculating machine for?
a: For his father, a tax official
92185.e: As a tax official, Pascal's father had to add up a great many numbers. The machine was meant to make this work easier for him.
92185.m: Pascal built the Pascaline to help his father with calculations.

92186.q: In which century did Blaise Pascal build his calculating machine?
92186.e: Pascal presented his calculating machine in 1645. That was in the 17th century, long before there was electricity in everyday life.
92186.m: The Pascaline was made in the 17th century.

92187.q: Which kind of calculation could the Pascaline carry out directly?
92187.e: The Pascaline was mainly an adding machine. Subtraction was only possible in a roundabout way using complement numbers.
92187.m: The Pascaline could mainly add numbers.

92188.q: How did you set the numbers on the Pascaline?
92188.e: There was a dial for each place. The result appeared in small windows above the dials.
92188.m: On the Pascaline you turned dials to enter numbers.

92189.q: Was the Pascaline an electric or a mechanical machine?
92189.e: In the 17th century there was no electricity in everyday life yet. The Pascaline worked purely mechanically with wheels and levers.
92189.m: The Pascaline was a purely mechanical calculating machine.

92190.q: Pascal built about 50 test models of his calculating machine. What does this show?
a: It took a lot of trying out before it worked well
He got the machine right at the first attempt
He wanted to give away 50 machines
92190.e: Pascal improved his machine again and again until it calculated reliably. Inventing often means trying things out, finding mistakes and improving.
92190.m: Pascal built about 50 test models of his calculating machine.

92191.q: When adding, what did a calculating machine like the Pascaline have to pass on automatically when a place went over 9?
92191.e: When a wheel jumps from 9 to 0, the next wheel has to be turned on by one. This is called carrying.
92191.m: When carrying, a one is passed on to the next place.

92192.q: How is information stored on a punched card?
92192.e: Whether there is a hole in a place or not carries the information. A machine senses the holes.
92192.m: A punched card stores data with holes.

92193.q: For which machine were punched cards already used around 1805 to control patterns?
92193.e: Joseph-Marie Jacquard used punched cards to control which threads were lifted during weaving. This created complicated fabric patterns automatically.
92193.m: Even looms were controlled with punched cards.

92194.q: What did Herman Hollerith use punched cards for in the USA in 1890?
92194.e: Hollerith developed machines that counted punched cards with details of each person. This meant the 1890 census could be analysed much faster.
92194.m: Hollerith counted the 1890 US census with punched cards.

92195.q: Which well-known computer company grew out of Herman Hollerith's firm?
92195.e: In 1911 Hollerith's firm became part of a merger which from 1924 was called International Business Machines (IBM).
92195.m: IBM grew out of Herman Hollerith's firm.

92196.q: What did you have to do if you had punched a wrong hole in a punched card?
92196.e: A punched hole cannot be closed again. That is why you punched the whole card again.
92196.m: Mistakes on punched cards could not be deleted.

92197.q: What happened if a programmer dropped a stack of punched cards?
a: The order of the program lines got mixed up
92197.e: Often one line of a program was on one card. So the order was important, and many programmers numbered their cards.
92197.m: With punched cards the correct order was very important.

92198.q: What was the device called that punched holes in punched cards?
92198.e: With a card punch you typed in characters, and the device punched the matching holes in the card.
92198.m: With a card punch you punched the holes in the card.

92199.q: What was one advantage of punched cards over handwritten lists?
a: Machines could read and sort them automatically
You could read them under water
92199.e: Punched cards could be counted, sorted and analysed by machines. This saved a lot of manual work.
92199.m: Punched cards could be read by machines.

92200.q: Which country did Charles Babbage come from?
92200.e: Charles Babbage was born in London in 1791. He was a mathematician, inventor and professor at Cambridge.
92200.m: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician.

92201.q: Which nickname is Charles Babbage often given?
92201.e: In the 19th century, Babbage designed calculating machines that already anticipated important parts of today's computer.
92201.m: Charles Babbage is considered the father of the computer.

92202.q: What was the name of Babbage's machine that was meant to calculate mathematical tables without errors?
92202.e: The Difference Engine was meant to calculate tables of numbers automatically. At that time, tables calculated by hand often contained errors.
92202.m: Babbage's Difference Engine was meant to calculate tables without errors.

92203.q: What was the name of Babbage's design for a freely programmable calculating machine?
92203.e: The Analytical Engine already had a calculating unit and a memory. It is considered a forerunner of the computer.
92203.m: The Analytical Engine was Babbage's design for a computer.

92204.q: Was the Analytical Engine completed during Babbage's lifetime?
a: Yes, there was one in every school
92204.e: The machine was too complicated and too expensive for the technology of the time. Babbage died in 1871 without completing it.
92204.m: Babbage's Analytical Engine was never completed.

92205.q: Which museum built a working Difference Engine from Babbage's plans in 1991?
a: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
92205.e: The Science Museum in London built Difference Engine No. 2 from Babbage's drawings. It worked and proved that his plans were correct.
92205.m: Babbage's Difference Engine works, as a reconstruction from 1991 shows.

92206.q: How were Babbage's calculating machines meant to be powered?
a: Mechanically, with gears and a crank or steam power
92206.e: Babbage's machines consisted of thousands of gears and shafts. Electricity was not yet available as a power source.
92206.m: Babbage's machines were mechanical and had many gears.

92207.q: Into which two main parts did Babbage divide his Analytical Engine?
92207.e: Babbage called the calculating unit the “Mill” and the memory the “Store”. This division can still be found in today's computers.
92207.m: Babbage divided his machine into a calculating unit and a memory.

92208.q: Which title is Ada Lovelace often given in the history of computing?
92208.e: In her notes she described an exact sequence of steps for how a machine should carry out a calculation. This is considered the first computer program.
92208.m: Ada Lovelace is considered the first programmer.

92209.q: For which machine did Ada Lovelace write her famous program in 1843?
a: For a calculating machine by Charles Babbage
92209.e: Ada Lovelace wrote a step-by-step plan for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. The program was meant to calculate the Bernoulli numbers.
92209.m: Ada Lovelace wrote a program for the Bernoulli numbers.

92210.q: Which programming language was named in honour of Ada Lovelace?
92210.e: The programming language Ada was developed around 1980 for the US Department of Defense and named after her.
92210.m: The programming language Ada bears the name of Ada Lovelace.

92211.q: What did Ada Lovelace foresee for calculating machines?
a: That they could not only calculate but also, for example, process music
92211.e: She realised that a machine like this could work with all kinds of symbols, such as musical notes. That was a very modern idea.
92211.m: Ada Lovelace realised that machines can process more than just numbers.

92212.q: Who is honoured on the yearly Ada Lovelace Day?
92212.e: Ada Lovelace Day takes place on the second Tuesday in October. It celebrates women in science and technology.
92212.m: On Ada Lovelace Day women in technology and science are honoured.

92213.q: Which computer did Konrad Zuse complete in Berlin in 1941?
92213.e: The Z3 is considered the world's first working, program-controlled and fully automatic digital computer.
92213.m: Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941.

92214.q: Which number system did Konrad Zuse's computers calculate with?
92214.e: Zuse used the binary system with only two digits, 0 and 1. This suits switches that are on or off.
92214.m: Zuse calculated with the binary system of zeros and ones.

92215.q: Which electrical components did the Z3 mainly consist of?
92215.e: The Z3 contained about 2000 relays. These are electromagnetic switches that clicked audibly while calculating.
92215.m: The Z3 calculated with clicking relays.

92216.q: What was Konrad Zuse's Z1 from 1938?
92216.e: The Z1 consisted of thousands of sheet metal parts and worked mechanically. It was often unreliable, because the parts got jammed.
92216.m: Zuse's first computer, the Z1, was mechanical.

92217.q: What happened to Zuse's Z3 in 1943?
a: It was destroyed in a bombing raid
It was put on display in a museum
It was mounted on a rocket
92217.e: During the Second World War the Z3 was destroyed in an air raid on Berlin. Today there are reconstructions.
92217.m: The original Z3 was destroyed in the Second World War.

92218.q: What did Konrad Zuse design in the 1940s besides his computers?
92218.e: Zuse designed Plankalkül, a language for programming computers. It is considered the first high-level programming language.
92218.m: Konrad Zuse also designed a programming language.

92219.q: Which university rented Zuse's Z4 computer in 1950?
92219.e: ETH Zurich rented the Z4 from 1950 to 1955. This meant one of the first computers in Europe was in Switzerland.
92219.m: Zuse's Z4 was at ETH Zurich from 1950 to 1955.

92220.q: In which country was the ENIAC built?
92220.e: The ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia and presented to the public in 1946.
92220.m: The ENIAC was built in the USA.

92221.q: In which year was the ENIAC presented to the public?
92221.e: The ENIAC was shown to the public on 14 February 1946. It was built from 1943 onwards.

92222.q: Which components did the ENIAC calculate with?
92222.e: The ENIAC contained about 17,500 valves. That is why it was much faster than computers with mechanical parts.

92223.q: Roughly how heavy was the ENIAC?
92223.e: The ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes and filled a whole large room.
92223.m: The ENIAC was as heavy as several lorries.

92224.q: What was the ENIAC originally meant to do calculations for?
a: For flight path tables for the US Army
92224.e: The US Army needed tables showing how shells fly. These ballistic calculations took a very long time by hand.
92224.m: The ENIAC first did calculations for the US Army.

92225.q: How was the ENIAC programmed at first?
a: By replugging cables and setting switches
92225.e: For every new task, cables had to be reconnected and rotary switches set. This could take days.
92225.m: The ENIAC was programmed with cables and switches.

92226.e: The first programmers of the ENIAC were women such as Jean Bartik and Betty Holberton. Today they are called the “ENIAC women”.
92226.m: The ENIAC was mainly programmed by women.

92227.q: What does the abbreviation ENIAC stand for?
a: European Network for Internet And Computing
92227.e: ENIAC means Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer.
92227.m: ENIAC is the abbreviation for an electronic computer.

92228.q: What does the name ERMETH stand for?
a: First calculating machine with electrical engineering
92228.e: ERMETH is short for the German “Elektronische Rechenmaschine der ETH”, the electronic calculating machine of ETH. It was developed in Zurich.
92228.m: The ERMETH was the calculating machine of ETH Zurich.

92229.q: What is special about the ERMETH for Switzerland?
a: It was the first computer built in Switzerland
It was the first pocket calculator
It was the first games console
92229.e: The ERMETH was developed and built at ETH Zurich itself. It is considered the first computer from Switzerland.
92229.m: The ERMETH was the first computer built in Switzerland.

92230.q: In which city was the ERMETH built?
92230.e: The ERMETH was created in the 1950s at ETH Zurich under the direction of the mathematician Eduard Stiefel.
92230.m: The ERMETH was built at ETH in Zurich.

92231.q: What served as the ERMETH's working memory?
92231.e: The memory was a magnetic drum weighing about 1.5 tonnes. It turned 100 times per second.
92231.m: The ERMETH stored data on a magnetic drum.

92232.q: Roughly how many valves did the ERMETH's calculating unit contain?
92232.e: The ERMETH's calculating unit consisted of about 1500 valves.
92232.m: The ERMETH calculated with about 1500 valves.

92233.q: Where can you see the ERMETH today?
a: In the Museum of Communication in Bern
In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
In the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
In the Federal Palace in Bern
92233.e: Since 2006 the ERMETH has been on permanent loan from ETH to the Museum of Communication in Bern. Before that it was in the Technorama in Winterthur.
92233.m: Today the ERMETH is in the Museum of Communication in Bern.

92234.q: Why was the ERMETH replaced after a few years?
a: Newer computers were faster and smaller
It was made of wood and rotted
Nobody wanted to calculate any more
92234.e: Computer technology developed at great speed. In 1963 a more modern computer replaced the ERMETH at ETH.
92234.m: Old computers are replaced by faster and smaller ones.

92235.q: Which number system did the ERMETH calculate with?
92235.e: The ERMETH worked with decimal numbers. One memory word had 16 decimal places.
92235.m: The ERMETH calculated with decimal numbers.

92236.q: Which country did the well-known computer scientist Niklaus Wirth come from?
92236.e: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur in 1934. Later he taught for many years at ETH Zurich.
92236.m: Niklaus Wirth was a Swiss computer scientist.

92237.q: At which university was Niklaus Wirth a professor of computer science from 1968 to 1999?
92237.e: Wirth taught for over 30 years at ETH Zurich and shaped computer science education there.
92237.m: Niklaus Wirth was a professor of computer science at ETH Zurich.

92238.q: Which important computer science award did Niklaus Wirth receive in 1984?
a: A gold medal at the Olympic Games
92238.e: The Turing Award is considered the “Nobel Prize of computing”. Wirth was the first German-speaking computer scientist to receive it.
92238.m: Niklaus Wirth received the Turing Award in 1984.

92239.q: What is the Swiss Niklaus Wirth famous for?
92239.e: At ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth developed programming languages such as Pascal and Oberon. Many people around the world learnt to program with Pascal.
92239.m: Niklaus Wirth developed programming languages such as Pascal.

92240.q: What did the computer that Niklaus Wirth's team built at ETH around 1980 already have back then?
a: A graphical screen and a mouse
92240.e: The computer was called Lilith. A screen with graphics and a mouse were new and rare at that time.
92240.m: Wirth's computer Lilith already had a mouse around 1980.

92241.q: Niklaus Wirth criticised the fact that programs keep getting bigger and more sluggish. What do you therefore often notice with new computers?
a: They still do not feel much faster
They no longer need any electricity
They can no longer open programs
92241.e: The hardware keeps getting faster, but the programs keep getting bigger too. That is why new computers often hardly feel faster.
92241.m: Big, sluggish programs slow down even fast computers.

92242.q: Which country did the famous computer scientist Niklaus Wirth come from?
92242.e: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur and taught at ETH Zurich. He is one of the best-known computer scientists in the world.
92242.m: Niklaus Wirth was a Swiss computer scientist.

92243.q: What is Niklaus Wirth mainly known for?
a: He invented programming languages such as Pascal
92243.e: At ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth developed several programming languages. The best known is Pascal.
92243.m: Niklaus Wirth invented the programming language Pascal.

92244.q: Who developed the programming language Pascal?
92244.e: Niklaus Wirth developed Pascal at ETH Zurich. Before that he had already worked on the language Algol W.
92244.m: The language Pascal comes from Niklaus Wirth.

92245.q: Who was the programming language Pascal named after?
92245.e: The language honours the French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal, who lived in the 17th century.
92245.m: Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal.

92247.q: What was Pascal especially popular for?
92247.e: Pascal was deliberately built in a clear way. That is why the language was used for teaching at schools and universities around the world.
92247.m: Pascal was a popular language for teaching programming.

a: An operating system for mobile phones
92248.e: Pascal is a programming language. With it you write commands that a computer can carry out.

92249.q: Which words begin and end a block of instructions in Pascal?
92249.e: In Pascal you group several instructions together between begin and end. The main program ends with end and a full stop.
92249.m: In Pascal, blocks go between begin and end.

92250.q: What did you need a program like Turbo Pascal for?
a: To write and run programs in Pascal
92250.e: Turbo Pascal was a development environment. In it you could write, compile and run Pascal programs.
92250.m: Many people programmed on the PC with Turbo Pascal.

92251.q: Which command in Pascal outputs text on the screen and moves to the next line?
92251.e: The command writeln stands for “write line”. For example, writeln('Hello') outputs the word Hello.
92251.m: In Pascal you output text with writeln.

92252.q: Which organisation did Grace Hopper work for for a long time, finally becoming an admiral?
92252.e: Grace Hopper joined the US Navy during the Second World War. She rose to the rank of rear admiral.
92252.m: Grace Hopper was a computer scientist and an admiral in the US Navy.

92253.q: What did Grace Hopper develop in 1952 as one of the first programs of its kind?
92253.e: A compiler automatically translates program text into machine language. Hopper's A-0 is considered one of the first compilers.
92253.m: Grace Hopper developed one of the first compilers.

92254.q: What did Grace Hopper want to achieve with her programming languages?
a: That programs could be written with words that are almost English
That computers would run without electricity
That only soldiers would be allowed to program
That programs would consist only of numbers
92254.e: Hopper thought programs should be readable for people. That is why the language COBOL, which she shaped, uses many English words.
92254.m: Grace Hopper wanted to make programs as readable as English.

92256.q: What did Grace Hopper like to show with a piece of wire about 30 centimetres long?
a: How far light travels in a nanosecond
How long a computer cable has to be
How thick a punched card is
92256.e: Light travels about 30 centimetres in a billionth of a second. This was her way of showing why short wires make computers faster.
92256.m: In a nanosecond light only travels about 30 centimetres.

92257.e: Because of her achievements and her manner she was often called “Amazing Grace”, after a well-known song.

92258.q: How big was the Harvard Mark I, which Grace Hopper worked on from 1944?
a: So big that it filled a whole room
As small as a mobile phone
As big as a school exercise book
92258.e: The Harvard Mark I was a huge electromechanical computer, about 15 metres long. Hopper was one of its first programmers.
92258.m: The first large computers filled whole rooms.

92259.q: In which century was Grace Hopper born?
92259.e: Grace Hopper was born in New York in 1906 and died in 1992. 1906 belongs to the 20th century.

92260.q: Which country does the company Logitech come from?
92260.e: Logitech was founded in 1981 in the canton of Vaud. Today the company sells its products all over the world.
92260.m: Logitech is a company from Switzerland.

92261.q: In which Swiss canton was Logitech founded?
92261.e: Logitech was founded on a farm in Apples in the canton of Vaud. Its registered head office is still in Vaud today.
92261.m: Logitech comes from the canton of Vaud.

92262.q: Which products is Logitech especially known for?
92262.e: Logitech mainly makes accessories for computers, especially mice and keyboards, as well as webcams and headsets.
92262.m: Logitech is known for mice and keyboards.

92263.q: Which device for video calls does Logitech make, among other things?
92263.e: A webcam is a small camera for the computer. Logitech is one of the best-known makers of such cameras.

92264.q: How did an early computer mouse detect how you moved it?
a: With a ball underneath that turned with it
92264.e: Early mice such as the first Logitech mouse from 1982 had a ball underneath. Today mice measure movement with light.
92264.m: Early computer mice had a ball.

92265.q: What does a wireless mouse need in order to work?
a: A battery or a rechargeable battery
92265.e: Without a cable the mouse gets no power from the computer. That is why it has a battery or rechargeable battery built in.
92265.m: Wireless mice need a battery or a rechargeable battery.

92266.q: Which product did Logitech bring onto the market in 1991?
92266.e: In 1991 Logitech brought out one of the first wireless radio mice, the Cordless MouseMan.
92266.m: Logitech brought out a wireless mouse in 1991.

92267.q: What do you need a Logitech headset for?
a: For listening and speaking, for example in video calls
92267.e: A headset is a pair of headphones with a microphone. You use it, for example, for gaming or in video calls.
92267.m: A headset is a pair of headphones with a microphone.

92268.q: What was a home computer in the 1980s?
a: An inexpensive computer for the home
92268.e: Home computers were affordable computers for families. People used them for playing, learning and programming.
92268.m: Home computers brought the computer into living rooms.

92269.q: What did home computers of the 1980s have compared with today's computers?
92269.e: Home computers often had only a few dozen kilobytes of working memory. A mobile phone today has many millions of times more.
92269.m: Home computers had very little memory.

92270.q: Which programming language was built straight into many home computers?
92270.e: After switching on, a BASIC interpreter often appeared straight away. This meant you could write your own programs immediately.
92270.m: Many home computers started directly with BASIC.

92271.q: What did people often connect home computers to as a screen?
92271.e: A separate monitor was expensive. That is why home computers were often connected to the television at home.
92271.m: Home computers were often connected to the television.

92272.q: On which storage medium were programs often saved on early home computers?
92272.e: With a cassette recorder, programs were saved as sounds on cassettes. Loading often took several minutes.
92272.m: Early home computers saved programs on cassettes.

92273.q: Which Apple computer came out in 1977 and became one of the first successful home computers?
92273.e: The Apple II appeared in 1977 with colour graphics and a keyboard. It was one of the first computers sold fully assembled.
92273.m: The Apple II from 1977 was an early successful computer.

92274.q: How did you operate most home computers of the early 1980s?
a: With the keyboard and typed commands
With your finger on the screen
92274.e: Most early home computers did not yet have a mouse. You typed commands such as LOAD or RUN on the keyboard.
92274.m: Early home computers were operated with typed commands.

92275.q: What did people often use to control games on home computers?
92275.e: A joystick is a control stick with a fire button. It was connected to the home computer and was very popular for games.
92275.m: Home computer games were often controlled with a joystick.

92276.e: The ENIAC was created at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. The building work was led by the engineers Eckert and Mauchly.
92276.m: The ENIAC was built at a university in the USA.

92277.q: In which city was Konrad Zuse born in 1910?
92277.e: Konrad Zuse was born in Berlin on 22 June 1910. He died in 1995.
92277.m: Konrad Zuse was born in Berlin in 1910.

92278.q: Which job did Charles Babbage have, among others?
92278.e: Babbage was professor of mathematics at Cambridge from 1828 to 1839. Isaac Newton had once held the same post.
92278.m: Babbage was a professor of mathematics at Cambridge.

92279.q: Which noble title did Ada Lovelace have?
92279.e: Through her marriage to William King, later the Earl of Lovelace, she became Countess of Lovelace. That is where her well-known name comes from.
92279.m: Ada Lovelace was an English countess.

92280.q: What colour are most carrots in the shop?
92280.e: Most carrots here are orange. But there are also yellow, white and purple varieties.

92282.q: Which canton is often called “Rüebliland” (carrot country)?
92282.e: Lots of carrots have been grown in Aargau for a long time. That is why it is also called Rüebliland, carrot country.

92283.q: Which cake is baked with grated carrots?
92283.e: Rüeblitorte is a well-known Swiss cake. The mixture contains finely grated carrots.

92284.q: Which substance gives the carrot its orange colour?
92284.e: The pigment carotene colours the carrot orange. Its name even comes from the word carrot.

92285.q: What colour were many carrots in the past, before there were orange varieties?
92285.e: The first carrots were often purple or yellow. Orange varieties were only bred later.
92285.m: In the past many carrots were purple or yellow.

92286.q: What part of the carrot grows above the ground?
92286.e: Above the ground you only see the green tops with finely feathered leaves. The orange root is in the soil.
92286.m: Carrot tops have finely feathered leaves.

92287.q: Carrots are good for one part of our body. Which one?
92287.e: Carrots contain a substance that the body turns into vitamin A. Our eyes need it to see.
92287.m: Carrots are good for your eyes.

92288.q: When does a carrot flower if you leave it in the ground?
92288.e: The carrot is a biennial. In the first year the root grows, and in the second year it flowers and makes seeds.
92288.m: The carrot only flowers in its second year.

92291.q: What is traditionally eaten with melted raclette cheese?
92291.e: Raclette comes with potatoes boiled in their skins. There are often pickled gherkins and silverskin onions too.

92292.q: Can you eat the small green berries of the potato plant?
92292.e: After flowering, small green berries form. They contain poison and must not be eaten.
92292.m: The berries of the potato plant are poisonous.

92293.q: What colour are potato flowers often?
92293.e: Potatoes flower in summer. Depending on the variety, the flowers are white, pink or purple.
92293.m: Potatoes have white or purple flowers.

92294.q: Where is the best place to store potatoes?
92294.e: Potatoes are stored in a cool, dark place, for example in the cellar. That way they sprout less quickly.
92294.m: Store potatoes somewhere cool and dark.

92295.q: Which potato dish is cut into strips and deep-fried?
92295.e: For chips, you cut potatoes into strips. Then they are deep-fried in hot oil.
92295.m: Chips are deep-fried strips of potato.

92297.e: Young tomatoes are green at first. Only when they ripen do most of them turn red.

92298.q: Which tomato sauce do people often eat with chips?
92298.e: Ketchup is made mainly from tomatoes, sugar and vinegar. Lots of people eat it with chips.

92299.q: Which continent does the tomato originally come from?
92299.e: The tomato comes from Central and South America. Sailors brought it to Europe about 500 years ago.
92299.m: The tomato originally comes from America.

92300.e: Tomato plants have small yellow flowers. The tomatoes later grow from them.

92301.q: When are tomatoes usually planted outdoors in Switzerland?
92301.e: Tomatoes cannot cope with frost. That is why they are only planted outdoors after the “Ice Saints” in mid-May.
92301.m: Tomatoes are only planted outdoors after mid-May.

92302.q: What is usually spread on a pizza base first?
92302.e: Most pizzas get tomato sauce first. Then come cheese and other toppings.
92302.m: Tomato sauce goes on the pizza first.

92303.q: What are tomato plants in the garden often tied to?
92303.e: Tomato plants grow tall and the fruits are heavy. A cane supports the plant so that it does not snap.
92303.m: Tomatoes are tied to a cane.

92304.q: What are small, round tomatoes that you can easily eat whole called?
92304.e: Cherry tomatoes are as small as cherries, which is where they get their name.
92304.m: Cherry tomatoes are as small as cherries.

92305.q: Which part of a lettuce do we eat?
92305.e: With lettuce, you eat the tender leaves. The root stays in the ground.
92305.m: We eat the leaves of lettuce.

92306.q: Why is it called head lettuce?
a: Its leaves form a round head
It is as hard as a head
92306.e: The leaves grow tightly on top of each other and form a round shape. This shape is called a head.
92306.m: Head lettuce forms a round head of leaves.

92307.q: Which animals in the garden especially like to eat lettuce?
92307.e: Slugs and snails love tender lettuce leaves. They often eat at night and in damp weather.
92307.m: Slugs and snails like eating lettuce leaves.

92308.e: Lettuce is usually eaten raw as a salad. You wash the leaves well first.

92309.q: What do you add to lettuce to make it taste better?
92309.e: You mix the salad with a dressing made of oil, vinegar and seasoning. That makes it taste nicer.

92310.q: What happens to lettuce when it is hot for a long time?
a: It becomes as hard as wood
92310.e: In hot weather, lettuce grows a tall stem with flowers. This is called bolting, and the leaves become bitter.
92310.m: In hot weather lettuce shoots up.

92311.q: What colour are lettuce leaves usually?
92311.e: Most lettuces have green leaves. There are also varieties with reddish leaves.

92312.q: What is a young lettuce plant that you plant in the garden called?
92312.e: A small, young plant for planting out is called a seedling. Lettuce is often planted this way.
92312.m: A young plant for planting out is called a seedling.

92313.q: Which meadow flower is lettuce related to?
92313.e: Lettuce and dandelions both belong to the daisy family. Both have a white milky sap.
92313.m: Lettuce is related to the dandelion.

92314.q: What colour is the skin of a cucumber?
92314.e: The skin of the cucumber is green. Inside, the flesh is pale.
92314.m: The cucumber has a green skin.

92315.e: Cucumber plants have yellow flowers. The cucumbers grow from some of the flowers.

92316.q: What are small cucumbers pickled in vinegar called?
92316.e: Small cucumbers are pickled in vinegar with spices. That way they keep for a long time and are called cornichons.

92317.q: Which plant is the cucumber related to?
92317.e: Cucumbers and pumpkins are close relatives. Both have yellow flowers and grow on long vines.
92317.m: The cucumber is related to the pumpkin.

92318.q: What is a cucumber mostly made of?
92318.e: A cucumber is made almost entirely of water. That is why it is so juicy and refreshing.
92318.m: A cucumber is almost all water.

92319.q: How is a cucumber usually cut for cucumber salad?
92319.e: For cucumber salad, you cut or slice the cucumber thinly. That way it soaks up the dressing well.
92319.m: For cucumber salad you cut thin slices.

92320.q: What do you find inside a cucumber?
92320.e: In the middle of the cucumber there are lots of small, soft seeds. They are the seeds of the plant.
92320.m: A cucumber contains lots of small seeds.

92321.q: Where do cucumbers often grow in Switzerland so that they are warm enough?
92321.e: Cucumbers like it warm and humid. That is why many cucumbers grow in greenhouses.

92323.e: Most courgettes are dark green. There are also yellow varieties.

92324.q: Apart from the fruit, which part of the courgette plant can you eat?
92324.e: You can eat the big yellow flowers of the courgette. For example, people stuff them or fry them in batter.
92324.m: You can also eat courgette flowers.

92325.q: How does a courgette plant usually grow?
a: As a big bush with huge leaves
As a tall tree with branches
As a tuber under the ground
As a water plant in a pond
92325.e: The courgette plant usually grows like a bush and has very large leaves. The fruits grow low down on the thick stem.
92325.m: The courgette grows as a big bush.

92326.q: What does the Italian word “zucchini” mean?
92326.e: In Italian, the pumpkin or squash is called “zucca”. So zucchini means little pumpkins. In Britain they are called courgettes.

92327.q: What happens to a courgette that is not picked in time?
92327.e: Courgettes keep growing very quickly. If they are left on the plant, they become huge and their skin gets hard.

92328.q: Why does a family often need only a few courgette plants?
a: Each plant produces lots of fruits
They only grow every ten years
92328.e: A single courgette plant produces lots of fruits in summer. That is why a few plants are enough for a family.
92328.m: A courgette plant produces lots of fruits.

92329.q: What is the name of a vegetable dish from France with courgettes, tomatoes and peppers?
92329.e: Ratatouille comes from the south of France. Courgettes, tomatoes, peppers and aubergines are stewed in it.
92329.m: Ratatouille is a vegetable dish with courgettes.

92330.q: At which autumn festival do people carve faces into pumpkins?
92330.e: At Halloween at the end of October, people hollow out pumpkins and carve faces into them. A candle shines inside.
92330.m: At Halloween people carve pumpkin faces.

92331.q: Apart from the flesh, what else can you eat from a pumpkin?
92331.e: You can roast and eat pumpkin seeds. They are also pressed to make oil.

92332.q: How heavy can the biggest giant pumpkins at competitions get?
92332.e: The heaviest pumpkins in the world weigh more than a tonne. That is heavier than a small car.
92332.m: Giant pumpkins can weigh over a tonne.

92333.q: In which season are pumpkins harvested?
92333.e: Pumpkins grow all summer. In autumn they are ripe and are harvested.

92334.q: What colour is the Hokkaido pumpkin usually?
92334.e: The Hokkaido pumpkin is usually bright orange. You can cook and eat its skin too.

92335.q: What is a pumpkin actually, according to plant scientists?
92335.e: The pumpkin is a fruit with seeds inside. Because its rind is hard, it is called an armoured berry (a pepo).
92335.m: The pumpkin is a berry with a hard rind.

92336.q: Why should you not eat ornamental gourds?
92336.e: Ornamental gourds often contain bitter substances that are poisonous. They are only for decoration.
92336.m: Do not eat ornamental gourds, as they can be poisonous.

92337.q: How long can many whole pumpkins be stored somewhere cool and dry?
92337.e: The hard rind protects the pumpkin. That is why it can often be stored for months somewhere cool and dry.
92337.m: A whole pumpkin often keeps for several months.

92338.q: What is the case that peas grow in called?
92338.e: Peas grow in a long green pod. It is also called a shell.

92339.q: What colour are fresh peas usually?
92339.e: Fresh peas are green and slightly sweet. Dried peas can also be yellow.

92341.q: Which scientist did famous experiments on inheritance using peas?
92341.e: Gregor Mendel crossed lots of peas in his monastery garden. This is how he found rules for how characteristics are passed on.
92341.m: Gregor Mendel did research with peas.

92342.q: In which fairy tale is there a pea under lots of mattresses?
92342.e: In the fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, a real princess feels the little pea through lots of mattresses.
92342.m: The princess feels the pea through lots of mattresses.

92343.e: Peas are small round balls. They can easily roll away.

92344.q: How do fresh peas stay green for a long time after harvest?
a: They are put in the sun
They are put in warm water
They are left lying open in a room
92344.e: Peas are frozen quickly after harvest. This keeps them fresh and green for a long time.
92344.m: Frozen peas stay fresh for a long time.

92345.q: What is a pea actually, for the plant?
92345.e: The pea is the seed of the pea plant. If you put it in the soil, a new plant grows.

92346.q: Why must you not eat green beans raw?
a: They are too hard to bite
92346.e: Raw beans contain a poisonous substance. Cooking destroys it.

92347.q: What is the bean called that climbs up long poles?
92347.e: The climbing bean grows very tall. That is why long poles are pushed into the ground for it to climb up.
92347.m: The climbing bean climbs up poles.

92348.q: What is the bean called that grows low and does not need a pole?
92348.e: The dwarf bean grows as a small bush. It does not need anything to climb up.
92348.m: The dwarf bean grows low like a bush.

92349.q: What is the red bean that is often in chilli con carne called?
92349.e: The kidney bean is a red variety of the common bean. It gets its name from its kidney shape.
92349.m: The kidney bean is red and shaped like a kidney.

92350.q: How does the climbing bean climb upwards?
a: Its stem winds around the pole
92350.e: The climbing bean has no tendrils. Its whole stem winds round and round the pole.
92350.m: The bean winds its stem around the pole.

92351.e: Wax beans are yellow green beans. Their colour is like wax.
92351.m: Yellow beans are called wax beans.

92352.q: What are the dried green beans that people in Switzerland eat with the Bernese platter called?
92352.e: In the past, beans were dried so they could be eaten in winter. These dried beans are still part of the Bernese platter today.
92352.m: Dried beans are part of the Bernese platter.

92353.q: Which part of the plant do you eat with green beans?
a: The whole pod with the seeds
92353.e: With green beans you eat the young, tender pod together with the little seeds inside. You must cook them first.
92353.m: With green beans you eat the whole pod.

92354.q: What colour is a radish on the outside, usually?
92354.e: Most radishes are bright red on the outside. There are also white varieties.
92354.m: Radishes are usually red on the outside.

92355.q: What colour is a radish on the inside?
92355.e: Inside, the radish is white. Only the thin skin is red.

92356.e: Radishes contain hot substances that taste a bit like mustard. That is why they burn a little on your tongue.

92357.q: Roughly how long does it take from sowing to harvesting radishes?
92357.e: Radishes grow very quickly. You can harvest them just a few weeks after sowing.
92357.m: Radishes grow in a few weeks.

92358.q: What shape is a typical radish?
92358.e: The typical radish is small and round. But there are also longer varieties.

92359.q: Which bigger, white vegetable is the radish closely related to?
92359.e: The small red radish and the large white radish belong to the same plant species. Both taste peppery.
92359.m: The radish is related to the white radish.

92360.q: What happens to radishes that stay in the ground too long?
92360.e: If radishes stay in the soil too long, they go woody or spongy inside. Then they no longer taste good.

a: Yes, for example in a salad
92361.e: Radish leaves are edible. You can put them in salad, soup or pesto.
92361.m: You can eat radish leaves too.

a: White at the bottom, green at the top
Red at the bottom, yellow at the top
Black at the bottom, white at the top
92362.e: The lower part of the leek is white because it grows in the ground. At the top the leaves are green.
92362.m: Leeks are white at the bottom and green at the top.

92363.q: Which vegetable is the leek related to?
92363.e: Leeks and onions belong to the same plant genus. Both smell and taste similar.
92363.m: The leek is related to the onion.

92364.q: Which dish from the canton of Vaud is made with leeks and potatoes?
92364.e: Papet vaudois is a stew of leeks and potatoes. It is eaten with a Vaud sausage.

92365.q: Can you harvest leeks in the garden in winter too?
a: Yes, they can cope with cold
No, they freeze to death straight away
92365.e: Winter varieties of leek can cope with frost. So you can harvest them in winter too.
92365.m: You can harvest leeks in winter too.

92366.q: What do you do to make the white part of the leek longer?
92366.e: You pile soil up around the leek. Whatever grows in the dark stays white.
92366.m: Piling up soil keeps more of the leek white.

92367.q: Which country has the leek as its symbol?
92367.e: The leek is a national symbol of Wales. Scotland has the thistle and Ireland the shamrock.
92367.m: The leek is a symbol of Wales.

92368.q: Where is there often soil in a leek that you have to wash out?
a: In the middle of a stone
92368.e: As the leek grows, soil trickles between the leaves. That is why you cut the leek open and wash it well.
92368.m: Wash leeks well between the leaves.

92370.q: Why do your eyes water when you cut onions?
a: A substance from the onion irritates your eyes
92370.e: When you cut it, a sharp substance is released and rises into the air. It irritates your eyes and they water.
92370.m: A substance from the onion makes your eyes water.

92371.q: What is the famous onion market in Bern called?
92371.e: At the Zibelemärit, farmers sell lots of onions in Bern's old town. It is a big public festival.

92372.q: In which month does the Zibelemärit in Bern take place?
92372.e: The Zibelemärit is held every year in November. Then Bern's old town is full of market stalls with onions.

92373.q: What is plaited from onions and sold at the Zibelemärit?
92373.e: At the Zibelemärit you can buy beautifully plaited strings of onions. You can hang them up and store them for a long time.

92374.q: What colour is the dry skin of most cooking onions?
92374.e: Most onions have a golden brown, paper-thin skin. There are also red and white onions.
92374.m: Most onions have a golden brown skin.

92375.q: What does an onion taste like when you cook it slowly in the pan for a long time?
92375.e: When cooked slowly, the onion loses its sharpness. It goes soft and tastes sweet.

92376.q: Which kitchen herb is related to the onion?
92376.e: Chives and onions belong to the same plant genus. Chives have thin, hollow, tube-shaped leaves.
92376.m: Chives are related to the onion.

92377.q: What are the small onions that you put into the garden soil in spring called?
92377.e: Onion sets are small onions. You push them into the soil and they grow into big onions.
92377.m: Onion sets are pushed into the soil.

92378.q: What grows out of an onion that has been lying in the kitchen for a long time?
92378.e: An old onion starts to sprout. Green shoots grow out of the top.

92476.q: Which animal has horizontal, oblong pupils?
92476.e: Goats and sheep have oblong pupils that lie sideways. That way they can see a lot of their surroundings while grazing.

92477.q: What happens to the pupil in bright light?
92477.e: In bright light the pupil narrows. That way not too much light gets into the eye.
92477.m: In bright light the pupil gets small.

92478.q: What happens to the pupil in the dark?
92478.e: In the dark the pupil opens wide. That way more light can get into the eye.
92478.m: In the dark the pupil gets big.

a: It lets light into the eye
92479.e: The pupil is the window of the eye. Light can only get inside through it.
92479.m: Light enters the eye through the pupil.

92480.q: Why does the pupil look black?
a: Hardly any light comes back out of it
92480.e: Light passes through the pupil into the dark inside of the eye. Almost nothing comes back out, so it looks black.
92480.m: The pupil looks black because almost no light comes back out of the eye.

92481.q: What shape is the human pupil?
92481.e: In humans the pupil is a round circle. Some animals have other shapes.

92482.q: Which animal often has a narrow, slit-shaped pupil during the day?
92482.e: In cats the pupil becomes a narrow slit in bright light. In the dark it becomes almost completely round.
92482.m: Cats have slit-shaped pupils in bright light.

92483.q: Why do eyes sometimes look red in photos taken with a flash?
a: The flash hits the blood vessels in the eye
92483.e: The flash shines through the pupil onto the back of the eye, which has lots of blood vessels. The red light comes back into the camera.
92483.m: Red eyes in photos come from the flash.

92484.q: What is the coloured ring around the pupil called?
92484.e: The iris is the coloured part of the eye. It lies all around the pupil.
92484.m: The iris is the coloured ring in the eye.

a: It makes the pupil bigger or smaller
92486.e: The iris has tiny muscles. They change the size of the pupil like the aperture of a camera.
92486.m: The iris controls how much light gets into the eye.

92487.q: What does the Greek word “iris” mean?
92487.e: Iris is the Greek word for rainbow. In Greek myths, a messenger of the gods was also called Iris.

92488.q: What can the pattern of the iris be used for?
92488.e: The pattern of the iris is different in every person. That is why machines can recognise a person by their iris.
92488.m: Every person has their own iris pattern.

92489.q: Which see-through layer lies in front of the iris?
92489.e: The cornea is as clear as the glass on a watch. It protects the iris and helps us see sharply.
92489.m: The see-through cornea lies in front of the iris.

92490.q: What is the white of the eye called?
92490.e: The sclera is the tough, white outer layer of the eye. It surrounds the coloured iris.
92490.m: The white of the eye is the sclera.

92491.q: Which eye colour is the most common in the world?
92491.e: Most people on Earth have brown eyes. Blue and green eyes are much rarer.
92491.m: Brown is the most common eye colour in the world.

92492.q: Which of these eye colours is the rarest?
92492.e: Only a few people in the world have green eyes. Brown eyes are the most common.

92493.q: In which part of the world do especially many people have blue eyes?
92493.e: Blue eyes are fairly rare worldwide. But in countries like Sweden or Finland, a great many people have blue eyes.
92493.m: Many people in northern Europe have blue eyes.

92494.q: Who do you get your eye colour from?
92494.e: Eye colour is inherited. It depends on the genes from your mother and father.
92494.m: You inherit your eye colour from your parents.

92495.q: Can a person have two different eye colours?
92495.e: Some people have, for example, one blue eye and one brown eye. This is rare and usually harmless.
92495.m: Two different eye colours are rare.

92496.q: Is there a blue pigment in blue eyes?
a: No, the blue comes from scattered light
Yes, a blue pigment in the iris
Yes, a blue pigment from the blood
Yes, a blue pigment in the tears
92496.e: Blue eyes have only a little pigment. The blue appears because light is scattered in the iris, a bit like with the sky.
92496.m: Blue eyes have no blue pigment.

92497.q: What eye colour do many fair-skinned babies have at birth?
92497.e: At birth, many fair-skinned babies still have little pigment in the iris. That is why their eyes are often blue or grey.
92497.m: Many babies have blue or grey eyes at first.

92498.q: When can a child's eye colour still change?
a: In the first years of life
92498.e: The pigment in the iris keeps forming after birth. That is why eye colour can still get darker in the first years of life.
92498.m: Small children's eye colour can still change.

92499.q: What do the eyes of people with albinism often look like?
92499.e: People with albinism have very little pigment in their bodies. That is why their eyes are often light blue or have a reddish shimmer.
92499.m: With albinism the eyes are often very pale.

92500.q: What are tears mostly made of?
92500.e: Tears are almost entirely water. There are also small amounts of salt and other substances.

92501.e: The tear gland lies above the eye. It constantly makes tear fluid.
92501.m: Tears come from the tear gland.

a: Above the eye, towards the outside
92502.e: The tear gland sits at the top outer edge of the eye socket. From there the fluid flows over the eye.
92502.m: The tear gland is at the top outer side of the eye.

92503.q: What are tears good for, even when you are not crying?
92503.e: A thin film of tears always covers the eye. It keeps it moist and washes away tiny bits of dust.
92503.m: Tears keep the eye moist and clean.

92504.q: What can help with dry eyes?
92504.e: Artificial tears come as eye drops. They moisten the eye when there are not enough natural tears.
92504.m: Artificial tears help with dry eyes.

92505.q: Why does your nose often run when you cry?
92505.e: A small duct leads from the inner corner of the eye into the nose. When you cry, a lot of tear fluid flows into it.
92505.m: Tears flow through a duct into the nose.

92506.q: What do tears do to germs in the eye?
92506.e: Tear fluid contains substances that harm bacteria. That way tears protect the eye from infections.
92506.m: Tears protect the eye from germs.

92507.q: What is different when many newborn babies cry?
92507.e: In the first weeks babies often make few tears. That is why they often cry without wet eyes.
92507.m: Newborn babies often cry without tears.

92508.q: Roughly how many times a minute does a person blink?
92508.e: A blink only lasts a fraction of a second. We usually blink without noticing.
92508.m: We blink several times a minute without noticing.

92509.q: Why do people wear glasses with specially shaped lenses?
92509.e: Glasses bend the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina. That way you can see clearly again.

92510.q: What is the job called in which you fit and sell glasses?
92510.e: Opticians measure the eyes and make the right lenses. They fit the glasses to the face.
92510.m: You get glasses from an optician.

92511.q: What can you put directly on your eye instead of glasses?
92511.e: Contact lenses are small, thin shells. They sit directly on the cornea and work like the lenses in glasses.
92511.m: Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

a: You can only see in the dark
92512.e: Short-sighted people see things close up sharply, but things far away look blurred. Glasses can correct this.
92512.m: Short-sighted people see things far away blurred.

92513.e: Long-sighted people find it hard to see things close up sharply. They often see things far away better.
92513.m: Long-sighted people see badly close up.

92514.q: Why do many older people need reading glasses?
a: The lens of the eye gets stiffer
92514.e: With age the lens in the eye can no longer change shape so well. That is why many people over about 45 see blurred close up.
92514.m: Many people need reading glasses as they get older.

92515.q: What happens to glasses in winter when you come into a warm house?
92515.e: The cold lenses cool down the warm, moist air. Tiny water droplets form on the glass.
92515.m: Cold lenses steam up in warm air.

92516.q: What is the part of the glasses that rests on the nose called?
92516.e: The bridge joins the two lenses. It rests on the top of the nose and carries the weight of the glasses.
92516.m: The bridge of the glasses rests on the nose.

92517.q: What does an eye test check?
92517.e: An eye test measures how sharply someone sees. That shows whether glasses are needed.
92517.m: An eye test checks how well your eyes see.

92518.q: What do you often read on the wall during an eye test?
a: Symbols that get smaller and smaller
92518.e: The eye chart has symbols of different sizes. The smaller the symbols you can make out, the better you see.
92518.m: On the eye chart the symbols get smaller and smaller.

92519.q: Why do you cover one eye during an eye test?
a: Because those are the rules of the game
92519.e: Often one eye sees better than the other. That is why each eye is tested on its own.
92519.m: In an eye test each eye is tested separately.

92520.q: What do you have to say in an eye test with rings?
92520.e: In the eye test with Landolt rings, each ring has a small gap. You say whether it is at the top, bottom, left or right.
92520.m: In the ring test you show where the gap is.

92521.q: What are small children shown in an eye test instead of letters?
92521.e: Children who cannot read yet name pictures or show which way symbols point. That way their eyes can be tested too.
92521.m: Small children do the eye test with pictures.

92522.q: For which licence do you need an eye test in Switzerland?
92522.e: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive has to take an eye test. Only then do they get a learner driver's permit.
92522.m: You need an eye test to drive a car.

92523.q: What do we call how sharply someone sees?
92523.e: Visual acuity tells you how finely someone can make things out. It is measured in an eye test.
92523.m: An eye test measures visual acuity.

92524.q: Where can you have a simple eye test done?
92524.e: Opticians and eye doctors do eye tests. For detailed examinations you go to an eye doctor.
92524.m: You have an eye test at the optician's or the eye doctor's.

92525.q: What is the doctor who examines and treats eyes called?
92525.e: Eye doctors know all about diseases of the eyes. They can also operate on eyes.
92525.m: For eye problems you go to an eye doctor.

92526.q: Why does the eye doctor sometimes put drops in your eye?
92526.e: With a wide pupil the doctor can see better inside the eye. Afterwards your vision is a little blurry for a few hours.
92526.m: Special drops widen the pupil for the examination.

92527.q: What do you read on a chart on the wall at the eye doctor's?
a: Letters that get smaller and smaller
92527.e: The eye chart has letters or pictures that get smaller and smaller towards the bottom. That shows the doctor how well you see.
92527.m: The eye doctor uses the eye chart to check how well I see.

92528.q: What is a common inflammation called in which the eye turns red and itches?
92528.e: The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. When it is inflamed, the eye turns red and itches.
92528.m: With conjunctivitis the eye is red.

92529.q: What is a small, inflamed lump on the eyelid called?
92529.e: A stye is an infection of a small gland at the edge of the eyelid. It is red and sore and usually heals by itself.
92529.m: A stye is an inflammation on the eyelid.

92530.q: What is replaced in an operation for cataracts?
92530.e: With cataracts, the lens in the eye becomes cloudy. In the operation an artificial, clear lens is put in.
92530.m: With cataracts the cloudy lens is replaced.

92531.q: What should you do if something sharp has got into your eye?
a: Don't rub it and go to a doctor
92531.e: Rubbing can injure the eye even more. That is why you go to a doctor or to A&E straight away.
92531.m: With an eye injury, go to a doctor straight away.

92532.q: What does the eye doctor often give you for an eye infection?
a: A plaster cast on your leg
92532.e: Many eye infections are treated with drops or ointment. They are put straight into the eye.
92532.m: Eye infections are often treated with drops.

92533.q: What does having a squint mean?
a: The eyes look in different directions
92533.e: With a squint, the two eyes don't point at the same target. One eye turns inwards, outwards, up or down.
92533.m: With a squint, the eyes don't look in the same direction.

92534.q: What do children with a squint often have stuck over one eye?
92534.e: A special patch covers one eye for a few hours a day. This is a common treatment for a squint.
92534.m: An eye patch helps many children with a squint.

92535.q: Why is the better eye covered when someone has a squint?
a: So the weaker eye gets trained
92535.e: When the good eye is covered, the weaker eye has to work. That way it learns to see better.
92535.m: Covering the good eye trains the weaker eye.

92536.q: Why should a squint in children be treated early?
a: Otherwise one eye learns to see badly
Otherwise the eyes water all the time
92536.e: The brain can ignore the image from the squinting eye. If it is not treated early, this eye stays weak-sighted.
92536.m: A squint is best treated early.

92537.q: What can often help with a squint as well?
92537.e: Some children squint because they are long-sighted. The right glasses can then reduce the squint.
92537.m: Glasses can help with a squint.

92538.q: When is a slight squint still normal in babies?
a: In the first months of life
92538.e: Newborn babies first have to learn to use their eyes together. If the squint lasts longer, an eye doctor should take a look.
92538.m: A brief squint is normal in young babies.

92539.q: What does someone often see if they suddenly start to squint?
92539.e: The two eyes then send two different images. The brain can no longer put them together.
92539.m: A sudden squint can cause double vision.

92540.q: How many muscles move an eye from the outside?
92540.e: Six outer eye muscles pull on each eye. They work together so that both eyes look in the same direction.

92541.q: What is sometimes done for a very strong squint?
a: An operation on the eye muscles
92541.e: In the operation, eye muscles are shortened or moved. Afterwards the eyes are straighter.
92541.m: A strong squint can be operated on.

92542.q: What do good sunglasses protect the eyes from?
92542.e: Good sunglasses keep out the dangerous UV rays. They also soften dazzling light.

92543.q: Where are sunglasses especially important in Switzerland?
a: In the snow in the mountains
92543.e: UV radiation is stronger in the mountains. The snow also reflects a lot of light back into the eyes.
92543.m: You need sunglasses in the snow in the mountains.

92544.q: What can happen in the snow without sunglasses?
92544.e: Too much UV light can burn the cornea. The eyes then hurt badly and you can't see well for a while.
92544.m: Without sunglasses you risk snow blindness.

92545.q: Can you look straight at the sun with sunglasses on?
a: Yes, for as long as you like
92545.e: Even sunglasses don't protect enough against direct sunlight. The eye can be permanently damaged.
92545.m: Never look straight at the sun.

92546.q: What do you need to watch a solar eclipse?
92546.e: Eclipse glasses only let through a tiny part of the light. Ordinary sunglasses are far too bright for this.
92546.m: Only watch a solar eclipse with special glasses.

92547.q: Why are dark glasses without UV protection bad?
a: The pupil gets big and more UV gets in
92547.e: Behind dark lenses the pupil opens. If there is no UV filter, even more harmful radiation then gets into the eye.
92547.m: Sunglasses always need a UV filter.

92548.q: What do people often wear when skiing instead of sunglasses?
92548.e: Ski goggles fit tightly against the face. They protect against sun, wind and snow.
92548.m: People often wear ski goggles when skiing.

92549.q: On which surfaces does the sun reflect especially strongly?
a: On soil and sand in the shade
92549.e: Snow and water reflect a lot of sunlight. The light then also hits the eyes from below.
92549.m: Snow and water reflect sunlight strongly.

92550.q: What helps blind people read texts on a computer?
92550.e: A screen reader reads out the texts on the screen with a computer voice. Some devices also show the text in Braille on a strip you can feel.
92550.m: Screen readers read texts aloud to blind people.

92551.q: Who invented the dot writing system for blind people?
92551.e: He went blind as a small boy. At the age of 15 he developed a writing system made of dots, which is named after him.
92551.m: The dot writing for blind people is named Braille after its inventor.

92552.q: What is the largest number of dots that one Braille character has?
92552.e: A Braille character has six dots in two columns. Depending on which dots are raised, a different letter is formed.
92552.m: A Braille character has up to six dots.

92553.q: Which country did the inventor of the dot writing for blind people come from?
92553.e: The inventor was born in France in 1809. He lived and taught in Paris.
92553.m: The inventor of Braille came from France.

92554.q: What colour is the cane that blind people use?
92554.e: The white cane shows other people that someone is blind. It is used to feel the way ahead.
92554.m: Blind people use a white cane.

92555.q: What helps blind people find their way on the pavement?
92555.e: In Switzerland there are white guide lines with grooves on the ground. You can feel them with a cane or your feet.
92555.m: White guide lines with grooves lead blind people.

92556.q: Which senses help blind people find their way especially well?
92556.e: Blind people pay close attention to sounds and feel their surroundings. That way they make up for part of their missing sight.
92556.m: Blind people find their way using hearing and touch.

92557.q: Where do you often find Braille in everyday life?
92557.e: Many medicine packets have the name in Braille. That way blind people can tell them apart.

92558.q: What is a guide dog for the blind?
a: A dog that leads blind people safely
A dog that searches for avalanche victims
92558.e: A guide dog is specially trained. It leads its person safely around obstacles.
92558.m: A guide dog leads blind people.

92559.q: Which dog breed is often trained as a guide dog?
92559.e: Labradors are calm, friendly and like to learn. That is why they are often trained as guide dogs.

92560.q: What does a guide dog wear when it is working?
92560.e: The guide harness has a firm handle. Through it the person feels every movement of the dog.
92560.m: A guide dog wears a harness.

92561.q: Should you stroke a guide dog while it is working?
a: Yes, but only on the head
92561.e: A working guide dog has to concentrate fully on the way. Distracting it can be dangerous for its person.

92562.q: What does a guide dog do when something is in the way?
a: It leads its person around it
92562.e: A guide dog learns to recognise obstacles. It leads its person safely past them.
92562.m: A guide dog leads around obstacles.

92563.q: Where does a young guide dog live before it is trained?
92563.e: With the puppy-raising family, the young dog gets to know everyday life. After that the real training begins.
92563.m: Young guide dogs grow up with a puppy-raising family.

92564.q: Who decides when to cross the road?
92564.e: The person listens to the traffic and gives the command. The dog then leads them safely across.
92564.m: The person decides when to cross the road.

92565.q: What does a guide dog do in front of stairs?
92565.e: The dog stops in front of stairs and kerbs. That way its person knows a step is coming.
92565.m: A guide dog stops in front of stairs.

92566.q: What do most people who are called colour-blind have?
a: They can only see at night
92566.e: Only very few people are completely colour-blind. Most of them just find it hard to tell certain colours apart.
92566.m: Most colour-blind people only mix up some colours.

92567.q: Which colours are most often mixed up by people with colour vision deficiency?
92567.e: The most common form is red-green colour blindness. People with it see red and green as similar.
92567.m: Red and green are the colours most often mixed up.

92568.q: Who more often has red-green colour blindness?
92568.e: It is inherited in a way that makes it much more common in men. Women are only rarely affected.
92568.m: Men more often have red-green colour blindness.

92569.q: Roughly how many out of 100 men in Europe have red-green colour blindness?
92569.e: In Europe about 8 to 9 out of 100 men are affected. In women it is fewer than 1 in 100.
92569.m: About one man in twelve has red-green colour blindness.

92570.q: How do you test whether someone sees colours well?
a: With pictures made of coloured dots
92570.e: A number made of coloured dots is hidden in the test pictures. People who mix up certain colours cannot see it.
92570.m: A colour test shows numbers made of coloured dots.

92571.q: Where does red-green colour blindness usually come from?
92571.e: Red-green colour blindness is usually inherited. It is not catching and lasts a lifetime.
92571.m: Red-green colour blindness is usually present from birth.

92572.q: What are the sensory cells in the eye that see colours called?
92572.e: The retina has three kinds of these cells for different colours. If one kind is missing, you see colours differently.
92572.m: The cones in the eye see colours.

92573.q: How do colour-blind people know which traffic light is on?
a: By the position of the light
By the sound of the cars
92573.e: The order of the lights on traffic lights is always the same. Red is at the top, green is at the bottom.
92573.m: At traffic lights, the position of the light helps.

92574.q: Why do we see almost no colours at night?
a: The colour cells need a lot of light
92574.e: In the dark, mainly sensory cells that only tell light from dark are working. That is why everything looks grey at night.
92574.m: All cats are grey in the dark, because we can hardly see colours.

92575.q: Why does a banana look yellow?
92575.e: Light contains many colours. The banana skin swallows most of them and mainly reflects yellow back into our eyes.
92575.m: We see the colour that a thing reflects.

92576.q: Which colour reflects almost all light?
